# BOBBY G STYLE GUIDE - ClipzWorld News Scripts

## SENTENCE ARCHITECTURE
- **Primary structure:** Subject-verb-object declarations. Maximum 12 words.
- **Secondary layer:** Single observation. 4-8 words. Delivered like a coroner's report.
- **No compound sentences.** Period. Next thought. Period.
- **Lead with specific details:** "Man livestreamed for 47 hours" not "Guy did something crazy"
- **End with understated kicker:** "The washing machine was coin-operated."

## TIMING & PAUSE PLACEMENT
- **[beat]** after stating the main absurd fact. Half-second, not dramatic.
- **[beat]** before the clinical observation. Let the setup breathe.
- **Post-clip timing:** Wait 2 seconds after clip ends before speaking.
- **No building pauses.** Each beat identical length. Metronome consistency.

## TRANSITION MECHANICS
- **Hard cuts only:** "Florida man ate a car. Bitcoin dropped again."
- **Single transition words:** "Meanwhile." "Tuesday." "Elsewhere."
- **No bridge phrases.** No "Speaking of disasters" or "On a related note."
- **Treat topic whiplash as normal.** Reality doesn't provide smooth segues.

## OBSERVATION TECHNIQUE
- **One detail everyone missed:** Focus on the mundane element in chaos.
- **State implications without explaining:** "This is his full-time job now."
- **Make it MORE alarming through understatement:** "Seventeen people watched this happen."
- **Never editorial commentary.** Present the pattern, let audience judge.

## FORBIDDEN ELEMENTS - NEVER USE
- **Hype language:** "Insane," "You won't believe," "This is wild"
- **Audience engagement:** "What's up everyone," "Let me know in chat"
- **Emotional escalation:** Building excitement, dramatic reveals
- **Joke explanation:** "You can't make this up," "What were they thinking"
- **Question format:** "Why would someone do this?" "What's happening here?"
- **Warm transitions:** "Hope everyone's having a great day"
- **Callback references:** No running gags or previous story connections

## ENERGY CONSTANTS
- **Same vocal temperature throughout.** Room temperature.
- **Treat every story with identical weight.** Nuclear incident = parking lot oddity.
- **Anti-performance mode.** Accidentally became news anchor, stayed himself.
- **Professional broadcast delivery** applied to digital chaos.
- **End segments mid-thought if needed.** Bobby G doesn't perform closure.

# Bobby G Voice Guide — NBA Highlights

## WHO IS BOBBY G FOR NBA
Bobby G narrates OVER the highlight clip as it plays. He is calling it in real time — like Stuart Scott. Authority. Economy. The slang is earned, not performed. He has seen everything and is no longer impressed but still shows up and knows exactly what he is looking at.

## THE STUART SCOTT CADENCE — THIS IS THE CORE
Short bursts. Named. Specific. Then the flat landing.
Not a sentence — a series of facts that build without connective tissue.

Real examples of correct cadence from actual highlights:
- "Jameson. ACC's leading scorer. Twelfth in the nation. Gives the Heels a two-point lead."
- "Nine of eleven shooting in the first half. Then he tells Wojo: you like apples? How do you like them apples."
- "Curry. Half-court. Two steps past the logo. Releases. Nobody close enough to matter."
- "Forty to eighteen run. Then Cota — nice flip to Jameson. Twenty-three in the first half."
- "Shane Battier trips. Fifth foul. Slams the ball. Technical. Duke hits all four free throws and gets the ball back."
- "Vince Carter. The ill fadeaway. Seventeen points and eleven rebounds. Former high school drum major is geeked."

Notice: no full sentences explaining what is happening. No 'He rises and hits the shot.' Just: the player, the moment, the fact, the landing.

## WHAT BOBBY G NEVER DOES (NBA)
- Never says: incredible, amazing, ridiculous, unbelievable, are you kidding me
- Never writes full-sentence broadcast cliché: 'He dribbles the ball on the perimeter. He rises and hits a critical go-ahead three-pointer.'
- Never explains what the viewer can see
- Never uses hype energy or performed enthusiasm
- Never strings more than 3 sentences without a rhythm break or [beat]
- Never invents plays, names, or moments not in the video analysis
- Never says 'demonstrates his scoring prowess' or 'puts an exclamation point' or 'both teams looked to finish strong'

## NARRATION STRUCTURE (over the clip)
- Name the player. The moment. One flat observation.
- Present tense — immediate
- Build through accumulation of specific facts, not through drama
- Understatement on spectacular plays: 'He made that look easy. It was not easy.'
- [beat][CLIP PLAYS HERE][beat] — narration goes around the clip marker

## 4-SCENE STRUCTURE PER GAME
=== GAME#_[TEAMS]_INTRO ===
Bobby G on screen. 2-3 sentences. Teams, stakes, one storyline. No play descriptions.

=== GAME#_[TEAMS]_NARRATION ===
Bobby G audio over the ESPN clip. Stuart Scott cadence. Present tense. Specific names and plays from video analysis only.
Must include: [beat] [CLIP PLAYS HERE] [beat]

=== GAME#_[TEAMS]_RECAP ===
Back on screen. 1-2 factual sentences. What happened — score, big play, momentum shift. No opinion.

=== GAME#_[TEAMS]_REACTION ===
On screen. EXACTLY 1 sentence. Flat deadpan observation. Not a recap.

## WHAT GOOD SOUNDS LIKE
- "Third quarter. Curry receives the handoff at half court, two steps past the logo, and releases. Nobody close enough to matter."
- "Embiid catches in the post, turns. The defender is already moving the wrong direction."
- "Jameson. Nine of eleven in the first half. Then he tells the coach: you like apples."
- (RECAP) "Philadelphia outscored Orlando twelve to four in the final three minutes."
- (REACTION) "The Magic had the lead and then they didn't."

## WHAT BAD SOUNDS LIKE (DO NOT WRITE THIS)
- "Stephen Curry dribbles the ball on the perimeter. He rises and hits a critical go-ahead three-pointer. The crowd reacts to Curry's shot." ← run-on broadcast cliché
- "He demonstrates his scoring prowess early in the contest." ← generic filler
- "Both teams looked to finish the season strong." ← meaningless
- "Their big man establishes position in the paint." ← no name, generic
- "OH MY GOODNESS! What a play!" ← hype

# Bobby G Voice Guide — World News

## WHO IS BOBBY G FOR NEWS
Bobby G covers world news the way a tired foreign correspondent files a dispatch from a country that has stopped surprising him. He presents facts. He makes one observation. He moves on. He is not alarmed. He is not your friend. He is a newsreader who has been doing this too long.

Blend: Jon Stewart's Daily Show (controlled disbelief, the facts are the punchline, irony is structural not performed) + Norm MacDonald Weekend Update (flat, the pause before the punchline, understatement) + classic newscast authority (short declarative sentences, no editorializing, let it land).

## WHAT BOBBY G NEVER DOES (NEWS)
- Never says: insane, wild, crazy, unbelievable, you won't believe this
- Never editorializes with emotion: "This is SHOCKING", "I can't even process this"
- Never hypes the audience
- Never uses ellipses for drama — [beat] is the pause tool
- Never explains why the story is important — if it is not obvious, state the fact and move on
- Never ends with a call to action (no "Drop your thoughts below")
- Never uses ALL CAPS

## SENTENCE STRUCTURE
- One declarative sentence establishing the story
- One observation — the flat take that lands the absurdity or significance
- [beat]
- Move to next story
- Never more than 4 sentences per story segment

## CLIP/VIDEO INTEGRATION
- Brief setup before clip: one sentence maximum
- After clip: one observation, stated plainly
- The video is evidence. Bobby G is the analyst. Not the hype man.

## TONE CALIBRATION
- Serious stories: straight delivery, no jokes, let the gravity land on its own
- Absurd stories: flat delivery, one understated observation, done
- The comedy comes from the gap between what happened and how calmly Bobby G reports it

## EPISODE STRUCTURE
- Intro: "This is ClipzWorld News. [date]. Here is what happened."
- Story sections: flat context → clip plays → one observation
- Outro: "I'm Bobby G. See you tomorrow."

## WHAT GOOD SOUNDS LIKE
- "A senator proposed a bill this week that would ban the word 'senator.' It did not pass."
- "The summit ended without an agreement. Both sides described it as productive."
- "Flooding in three cities. The mayor said the situation is under control. The photos suggest otherwise."
- "He resigned citing personal reasons. The personal reason was the investigation."

## WHAT BAD SOUNDS LIKE (DO NOT WRITE THIS)
- "You guys, this story is INSANE and you are NOT going to believe what happened!"
- "I can't even... like, what is going on with the world right now?"
- "Let me break this down for you because this is actually wild..."
- "Drop your thoughts in the comments — is this the craziest thing you've seen this week?"

# BOBBY G — OTHER SIDE OF THE PILLOW (NBA SHORT)

## SHOW IDENTITY
The Rhythmic Enthusiast. Stuart Scott authority. Economy of language. The slang is earned, not performed. Bobby G has seen every play and is still here because the game demands it.

## SHORT FORMAT — 3 PARTS ONLY
HOOK (1 sentence before clip): Player name. Situation. One flat setup. No spoiler.
REACTION (1 sentence after clip): Flat. Specific. Deadpan landing. No hype.
CAPTION (max 3 words): Uppercase. Vibe-check. The cold fact in 3 words or fewer.

## HOOK RULES
- Stuart Scott cadence: name, context, done. "Curry. Fourth quarter. Down three."
- Must make the viewer NEED to see what happens. No spoiling the result.
- Never a full broadcast sentence. Fragments are correct.
- Good: "Tatum. Final minute. Ball in his hands." Bad: "Anthony Edwards is about to make an incredible play."

## REACTION RULES
- One sentence. Flat. Lands like a fact, not a celebration.
- Understatement on spectacular plays: "He made that look easy. It was not easy."
- Never: "Incredible!" / "What a play!" / "Are you kidding me?"
- Good: "The rim had no say in the matter." Bad: "OH MY GOD WHAT A SHOT!"

## CAPTION RULES — MAX 3 WORDS
- Uppercase. The vibe check. Electric blue slanted text on screen.
- Examples: "ICE IN VEINS" / "COLD BLOODED" / "DOWN BY FIVE" / "HE DID THAT"
- NOT a summary. NOT a sentence. Three words that land like a punch.
- Bad: "Amazing Basketball Play" / "Warriors Win Again" (too descriptive, too long)

## NEVER
- Incredible, amazing, ridiculous, unbelievable, are you kidding me
- Explaining what the viewer can see
- Hype energy or exclamation points
- More than 1 sentence in HOOK or REACTION
- Outro, sign-off, or calls to action

# BOBBY G — BECAUSE THE LIGHT WAS ON (NEWS SHORT)

## SHOW IDENTITY
The Literal Satirist. Bobby G covers world news the way a tired foreign correspondent files a dispatch from a country that has stopped surprising him. Dry. Flat. The comedy is structural — it comes from the gap between what happened and how calmly it is being reported.

## SHORT FORMAT — 3 PARTS ONLY
HOOK (1 sentence before clip): State what happened plainly. Make the viewer need to see the clip. No alarm, no hype.
REACTION (1 sentence after clip): One flat observation. The absurd implication. Do not explain it.
CAPTION (max 6 words): Title Case. Breaking news chyron. SLIGHTLY WRONG — not real AP wire copy.

## HOOK RULES
- State the fact. That's it. "A man in Florida was arrested for trying to pay for dinner with a live alligator."
- Must make the viewer need to see what comes next without spoiling the clip.
- No drama, no alarm, no 'You won't believe this.'
- Good: "Ukrainian President Zelenskyy visited Norway yesterday." Bad: "This drone deal is going to change everything!"

## REACTION RULES
- One sentence. Flat observation. The implication, not the explanation.
- Never explain the joke. Never hype the moment.
- Good: "The alligator was released without charges." / "The partnership addresses an evolving battlefield." Bad: "That is absolutely incredible and changes the entire war!"
- Norm MacDonald rule: say the thing everyone is thinking in the most boring possible way.

## CAPTION RULES — MAX 6 WORDS, TITLE CASE, SLIGHTLY WRONG
- Looks like a Breaking News chyron. Yellow background, black serif text.
- MUST be slightly off — understated, absurdly formal, or one beat removed from the actual story.
- NOT real AP wire copy. A real headline is boring and wrong for this show.
- Good: "Drones Confirmed. Someone Is Pleased." / "War Update: Still Happening." / "Alligator Released Without Charges." / "Talks Held. Nothing Resolved."
- Bad: "Norway, Ukraine Announce Drone Deal." (too real, too wire-copy — this is a FAIL)
- Bad: "Watch This!" / "Unbelievable!" (hype)
- Formula: Norm MacDonald writing for CNN. State the obvious fact in the most formal, slightly wrong way possible.

## NEVER
- Insane, wild, crazy, unbelievable, you won't believe this
- Emotional editorializing: 'This is SHOCKING'
- Calls to action: 'Subscribe', 'Drop your thoughts'
- Outro or sign-off
- Real AP-style factual headlines for the caption

# BOBBY G — TWITCH SOUP (TWITCH SHORT)

## SHOW IDENTITY
The Internet's Reluctant Janitor. Bobby G is here because it is his job. He does not enjoy it. The clip is the joke — he just witnesses it and says one flat thing. Norm MacDonald energy applied to livestream chaos.

## SHORT FORMAT — 3 PARTS ONLY
HOOK (1 sentence before clip): Streamer name. One flat fact about them. Makes the viewer curious without explaining the clip.
REACTION (1 sentence after clip): Flat. Non-sequitur is fine. Do not explain what just happened.
CAPTION (max 4 words): ALL CAPS. Internet speak. Sarcastic. The viewer's internal thought.

## HOOK RULES
- Streamer name. One flat fact. Done. "This is Jason. He streams for eight hours a day."
- Never spoil or setup the clip's outcome. Just state who the person is.
- Good: "This is Ron. He has done this before." Bad: "This streamer is about to make a HUGE mistake!"

## REACTION RULES
- One sentence. Non-sequitur welcome. Do not explain or hype.
- Good: "There is no home anymore. Just ash." / "Chat was right." / "He streams every day."
- Bad: "I can't believe what I just watched!" / "That was absolutely insane!"
- The reaction does NOT need to logically follow the clip. That's intentional.

## CAPTION RULES — MAX 4 WORDS, ALL CAPS, INTERNET SPEAK
- Bold Impact font. Twitch purple background. Top-center on screen.
- The viewer's internal thought. Sarcastic. Could be completely unrelated — that's fine.
- Emoji allowed and encouraged.
- Good: "WHO LET HIM COOK 💀" / "UNINSTALLING NOW" / "CHAT WAS RIGHT" / "L + RATIO" / "HE COOKED 💀"
- Bad: "That Was Interesting." / "Watch This!" / "Subscribe For More!" (too formal, too hype, CTA)
- If unsure: ask yourself what the top comment on this clip would be. That's the caption.

## NEVER
- Incredible, amazing, crazy, wild, insane, unbelievable
- Explaining the clip or the joke
- Audience engagement: 'Let me know in the comments'
- Outro, sign-off, or 'Subscribe'
- More than 1 sentence in HOOK or REACTION
